transcript:
This is NPR News Now, the latest headlines every hour.
>> Live from NPR News in Washington, I'm Windsor Johnston.
Airlines are working to get back on schedule this morning following Friday's nationwide ground stop.
The disruption left thousands of people stranded at airports across the country.
Passengers Elias Gordon and Bruce Wilson are driving to Pittsburgh after their flight was canceled.
>> I had to get home for a wedding. He has to get home.
We met at the terminal and the flights weren't going anywhere.
So we decided to get together, us two and one other guy, and rent a car and drive to Pittsburgh.
>> Federal officials say problems with radar and communications forced the FAA to halt departures.
NPR's Joel Rose reports Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy is blaming an outdated air traffic control system.
>> Duffy said the old equipment was overloaded by data, though he did not say why.
And reporters pushed him to explain what happened to overwhelm the FAA's systems on what seemed to be just a normal travel day.
He said investigators are still working on that.
Homeland Security Secretary Mark Wayne Mullen was asked repeatedly if this was a cyber attack.
He said it does not appear to be, though he also said, quote, there's nothing completely certain right now.
>> That's NPR's Joel Rose reporting.
The ground stop in the U.S. also impacted airports overseas with U.S.-bound flights delayed or canceled.
European air traffic control officials temporarily suspended departures to the United States.
Vicki Barfer reports from London.
>> The European Air Safety Agency Eurocontrol suspended U.S.-bound flights across all 42 of its member countries shortly after the FAA announced the groundings.
That suspension has now been lifted, but London's Heathrow Airport was among those still showing a number of both arriving and departing transatlantic flights as delayed or canceled Saturday.
Britain's Civil Aviation Authority has issued a statement warning travelers of follow-on disruption as airlines scramble to reposition aircraft and crews.
For NPR News, I'm Vicki Barfer in London.
>> FlightAware.com now lists more than 3,500 cancellations today for flights within, into or out of the U.S.
Residents near an ethanol plant in central Illinois remain out of their homes while authorities search for possible explosive devices.
Police say a suspicious package at the Bioerja Renewables Facility posed a credible bomb threat and has been neutralized.
FBI Special Agent in Charge Ryan Pressley spoke early this morning.
>> While it is early in the investigation, know this, we will work tirelessly to identify the individual responsible and bring them to justice.
>> The threat prompted overnight evacuations within a mile of the plant.
This is NPR News in Washington.
>> Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney says there's progress toward a trade deal with the United States.
Dan Karbinschuck reports Carney's comments came during his visit to Manila, where he's wrapping up negotiations on a free trade deal with the Philippines.
>> Carney says he and President Donald Trump recently held lengthy and substantive talks on a trade deal, though he says, quote, "We're not yet there."
U.S. Ambassador Pete Hoekstra has also said a deal could be reached by the end of the year.
The Prime Minister was speaking in Manila ahead of a three-day summit of Southeast Asian countries where he announced a new Canada-Philippines free trade agreement.
Carney said it's part of his strategy to reduce Canada's reliance on the U.S. as a trading partner.
He is also working towards a broader deal that would provide Canadian exporters with access to a market of nearly 700 million consumers across Southeast Asia.
For NPR News, I'm Dan Karbinschuck in Toronto.
>> The Trump administration says it will allow states to delay cutting off Medicaid coverage for people who fail to meet new work requirements.
States can postpone those coverage losses until July 1st rather than starting in January.
The requirements apply to certain adults who must work, volunteer, or participate in other qualifying activities unless exempt.
States choosing the delay must still check whether people meet the rules.
Federal officials say the extra time will help states improve their systems and avoid mistakes that could disrupt coverage.
I'm Windsor Johnston, NPR News, in Washington.

topics.text: Airlines recover from Friday's nationwide FAA ground stop that stranded thousands of travelers
Travelers Elias Gordon and Bruce Wilson drive to Pittsburgh after flight cancellation
Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy blames outdated air traffic control equipment for FAA ground stop
Homeland Security Secretary Mark Wayne Mullen says ground stop does not appear to be a cyber attack
European air safety agency suspends U.S.-bound flights across 42 countries, later lifted
Illinois residents evacuated from near Bioerja ethanol plant amid bomb threat investigation
Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney says progress made toward U.S. trade deal
Carney announces Canada-Philippines free trade agreement at Southeast Asia summit in Manila
Trump administration lets states delay Medicaid coverage cutoffs for failing new work requirements until July
